transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-09-16
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Samira Khan (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Jared Morris (Streamline Head of ML), Priya Patel (Platform Eng), Alex Chen (Data Privacy)

Summary (auto): Weekly POC sync focused on caching work. Reviewed KV/prefix cache hit rates, looked at prompt reuse patterns, discussed tradeoffs for TTLs and canonicalization, planned benchmarks and next steps for Dedicated pilot.

[00:00] Samira: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call — we've got Jared, Priya, Alex — hey — and Diego joining from the SE side. How's every — how's everyone doing?
[00:06] Jared: Good, thanks. Ready to go.
[00:08] Priya: All right here.
[00:10] Alex: Yep.
[00:12] Diego: Hey team.

[02:05] Samira: OK, agenda: quick refresher on where we left, Diego will walk through the hit-rate changes and what we changed in the prefix canonicalization, then we'll talk TTLs and cost/latency impact, then agree next steps.

[04:20] Diego: Cool. So, quick context — last week we noticed KV cache hit rates were low, like in the low teens, around 12% overall. We changed two things: 1) we applied a light canonicalization pass to prompt prefixes — whitespace normalization, lower-casing of user-provided metadata tokens — and 2) we grouped similar prompt templates into 3 buckets so we don't over-index on micro-variations. After those changes we saw combined KV + prefix hit go to about 46% across the test set.
[04:55] Jared: 46% wow that's a big jump. Is that across all intent types or just the high-frequency ones?
[05:05] Diego: Mostly the high-frequency ones — the top 20 templates. The long tail still has low reuse. So our effective global hit is around mid-40s but session-level varies.

[06:30] Priya: Can you show the dashboard? The link you sent earlier wasn't loading for me.
[06:35] Diego: Yeah, I pasted the dashboard again in chat; try now. (pause) Looks like it resolved. On the hit-rate graph you can see the pre-change baseline, the small bump when we enabled prefix trimming, and the larger bump after template bucketing. There's still noise though because some prompts include timestamps or UUIDs.

[08:18] Jared: About those UUIDs — is there a way to hash them or strip them before keying? That's a lot of churn.
[08:25] Diego: Absolutely. We recommended a fingerprinting step: either regex-based stripping of known payload fields or a parameterized canonicalizer that replaces long uuids/timestamps with placeholders before computing the KV key. That increases hit rate without changing model inputs.

[09:12] Samira: Quick question on safety / privacy — Alex, any concerns with us normalizing out customer tokens?
[09:20] Alex: The suggested approach is acceptable if we don't persist raw PII in the normalized keys. We want to ensure the placeholders are deterministic but non-reversible, and ideally the key hashing uses a KMS-backed HMAC so there isn't recoverable PII in logs. Does Redwood support that?
[09:40] Diego: Yes, we can HMAC keys with a KMS-provided key for the Dedicated and Private deployments. For Hosted we have a managed KMS option and audit logs; we can share the security docs.

[11:00] Priya: On TTL — you mentioned TTLs of 1 hour vs 24 hours. What's the tradeoff we saw in cost and staleness?
[11:10] Diego: Short TTLs like 1 hour gave high freshness but reduced hit rate — so per-request compute cost remained higher. 24-hour TTL increased hit rates by about 8-10% on top of canonicalization because repeated prompts across days are common. Cost per 1M tokens dropped ~12% in the 24h run vs 1h, latency median improved by ~30ms attributable to cache hits.

[12:40] Jared: Are there workloads where longer TTLs cause correctness issues — e.g., price lists or inventory prompts?
[12:48] Diego: Yes — for anything that is time sensitive, like pricing or ephemeral coupons, TTL must be short or there's a cache-bypass policy. We recommend classifying templates: stable vs volatile, and set TTLs per class. The Redwood console supports route-level TTLs.

[14:30] Priya: Implementation detail: our prompts have user context block, system instructions, and product lists. We typically re-order product lists sometimes; does that break cache keys?
[14:40] Diego: Order matters if the prompt text is used verbatim. Two options: 1) for product lists we canonicalize ordering (e.g., sort alphabetically or by SKU) before keying, or 2) embed a condensed signature for list content (e.g., a content-hash based on normalized set). Both approaches helped other customers.

[16:05] Jared: Can Redwood's client SDK do that transformation for us or we do it in our app?
[16:12] Diego: We have a light client preprocessor in the SDK that can do canonicalization hooks; for enterprise customers we can extend it. For Dedicated, you can also run canonicalization on the edge sidecar.

[17:30] Samira: Quick nit — Diego wrote in the last notes 'KV cash' a couple times, hope that didn't confuse folks.
[17:35] Diego: (laughs) yep, my bad.

[18:00] Alex: On audit/a11y — when we HMAC the key, we lose the ability to debug which prompt generated a key unless we keep an ephemeral mapping. Is there any recommended logging level?
[18:12] Diego: We usually recommend keeping a short-lived mapping in a secure logs store for debugging for up to 7 days, and ensuring mappings are encrypted and access-controlled. For enterprise/private setups we can keep longer retention per contract. We'll share the policy doc.

[19:40] Priya: About the long tail — any suggestions to capture reuse from paraphrases? People rewrite prompts slightly.
[19:45] Diego: Paraphrase normalization is hard. Two pragmatic options: 1) use a clustering approach offline to discover common paraphrase groups and then create canonical templates for them, 2) for real-time, use an approximate similarity-based keying — e.g., compute a fingerprint of semantic embedding and bucket by nearest neighbor; that increases false positives but catches paraphrases. We recommend doing offline clustering first to avoid over-hitting with false positives.

[22:10] Jared: Did you already try embedding-based bucket keys in the POC?
[22:15] Diego: We ran a small experiment: embedding-buckets increased hit-rate for paraphrased intents by ~6% but added latency on miss (embedding compute). Net cost benefit was marginal for their current traffic shape. We can re-run at scale.

[24:05] Samira: Let's review metrics slide — Diego?
[24:10] Diego: Sure. Pre-change: KV hit 12%, prefix hit ~18% (some overlap). Post-change: KV hit 35%, prefix hit 22%, combined effective hit ~46% as I mentioned. Median latency for generate calls dropped from 420ms to 360ms. 95th percentile improved modestly — from 980ms to 930ms. Cost estimate: roughly $0.85 per 1k requests saved after factoring batching improvements. Caveat: these are POC numbers on our sample traffic.

[26:00] Priya: Those p95 numbers seem... still higher than we hoped. Is that mostly model compute variance or infra?
[26:08] Diego: Mostly model compute on cold KV misses and some tail caused by long-running evals. We recommended enabling more aggressive batching on non-latency critical routes; that helps throughput and reduces p95 for background traffic.

[27:30] Jared: Can we set a policy to only batch on second-tier traffic? We can't risk user-facing latency.
[27:36] Diego: Yes, route-level configs allow you to set batching thresholds and latency SLOs, and Redwood can auto-fallback to single-request mode for routes tagged as low-latency critical.

[29:00] Alex: Security question: If we push to Dedicated, do we keep control over the HMAC key in our KMS?
[29:06] Diego: Yes — Dedicated supports customer-managed KMS (Bring-Your-Own-Key) so you control the HMAC material. For Hosted we offer managed KMS with strict controls, but key custody differs.

[30:10] Priya: For the upcoming benchmark we want to compare 8k vs 16k contexts — what should we be measuring beyond hit-rate and latency?
[30:18] Diego: Good question: measure token cost per successful user transaction, median/P95/P99 latency, model-quality deltas (we'll run a small eval set to check for generation regressions), and server-side resource utilization (GPU mem and throughput). Also track cache eviction rate and key churn.

[31:40] Samira: Action items recap in a minute. But quick pricing — Jared asked last time about bridge pricing for the Dedicated pilot. I can send a tailored quote if you confirm expected QPS and retention.
[31:55] Jared: We're aiming for a pilot at ~250 QPS peak with expected average 80 QPS, and about 1000 daily active users to start. We'll provide a more accurate number in the next day.

[33:10] Priya: On the canonicalization library — Diego, will you push a small sample into the repo for us to try?
[33:15] Diego: Yes, I'll attach a minimal node/python example for prompt canonicalization and a small docker sidecar that does HMAC keying.

[34:30] Jared: Weird question — any pitfall you saw when customers enable long TTLs and then update system instruction text? Will cache serve old system instructions?
[34:40] Diego: If system instruction changes should invalidate certain caches. We recommend including a system instruction version component into the cache key. For example, include a 'si_v1' tag in key. The console can manage rollout of those version tags.

[36:00] Alex: For compliance I'll ask: can we get a sample of the key-hash algorithm and the minimal security architecture? I'll take that offline.
[36:08] Diego: Absolutely; I'll drop the design doc and the KMS/HMAC options.

[37:20] Samira: Ok, let's do a quick recap and next steps.
[37:25] Samira: Items — I'll send pricing and config recommendations; Diego will run the 24h TTL bench and share dashboards + canonicalization examples; Priya will share prompt samples; Alex will review security doc. We'll also schedule the 8k vs 16k benchmark next week. Anyone object or want to add?
[37:45] Priya: Sounds good. Please include example regexes you used for UUID stripping.
[37:50] Diego: Will do.

[39:10] Jared: One more ask — can you include a rough rollout plan for applying canonicalization in prod? Staged deploy notes etc.
[39:18] Samira: Yes we'll include a staged rollout doc: dev -> canary -> prod with metrics to watch.

[40:30] Samira: All right thanks everybody. We'll follow up in email with attachments.
[40:36] Jared: Thanks.
[40:37] Priya: Bye.
[40:38] Alex: Bye.

End transcript.

Meeting recap (auto): 46% combined cache hit after canonicalization + template bucketing, recommended TTLs per template class (1h for volatile, 24h for stable), action items assigned, next benchmark scheduled for 8k vs 16k contexts.
